worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts pharmacist is rostered on a Sunday with four support personnel assisting in filling prescriptions: one certified pharmacy technician and three pharmacy technicians, every licence current and verified that morning. The scheduling manager says the shift is compliant because four is the maximum the regulation allows and nobody is over it. Is the roster within the supervisory ratio?
steps: Fix the counted population first. All four are within the categories named in 247 CMR 8.06(3)(a), and all four are assisting in filling prescriptions, so all four count.

Test the first route to four in 247 CMR 8.06(3)(a)1.a: at least one of the four is a certified pharmacy technician and one is a pharmacy intern. There is a certified pharmacy technician but no intern, so the condition fails.
Test the second route in 247 CMR 8.06(3)(a)1.b: at least two of the support personnel are certified pharmacy technicians. There is one, so the condition fails.
Test the third route in 247 CMR 8.06(3)(a)1.c: two of the support personnel are pharmacy interns. There are none, so the condition fails.

Drop to 247 CMR 8.06(3)(a)2, which permits three support personnel provided at least one of the three is a pharmacy intern or a certified pharmacy technician. The certified pharmacy technician satisfies that, so three of these four are supportable.
worked_examples.resolution: The roster is not within the ratio at four; on this composition the pharmacist may supervise three. The error the scenario invites is reading a maximum of four support personnel as a headcount allowance. Every one of the three routes to four is a condition on credential composition, and one certified pharmacy technician with no pharmacy intern satisfies none of them, however current the other three licences are.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacist works a shift with three support personnel who satisfy the applicable ratio: one certified pharmacy technician, one pharmacy technician and one pharmacy technician trainee. A cashier holding no Board credential rings front-store sales all morning. At noon the queue builds and the Manager of Record asks the cashier to key prescription data for an hour. What changes?
steps: Before noon, apply 247 CMR 8.06(3)(b). The cashier does not fall within the definitions of a pharmacy intern, certified pharmacy technician, pharmacy technician or pharmacy technician trainee, and is not supporting the pharmacist in any professional capacity, so both limbs of the exclusion are satisfied and the cashier is outside the count.

At noon the second limb fails. Keying prescription data is support of the pharmacist in a professional capacity, so the condition on which the exclusion depended is no longer met and the cashier is no longer excluded from the ratio.
Recount the support personnel: the certified pharmacy technician, the pharmacy technician, the pharmacy technician trainee and now the cashier make four.
Test the four-person conditions in 247 CMR 8.06(3)(a)1. There is one certified pharmacy technician and no pharmacy intern, so none of the three conditions is satisfied.

Note what the ratio does not decide. 247 CMR 8.06(3) is a rule about how many support personnel a pharmacist may supervise and in what credential mix; whether this particular person may lawfully perform prescription data entry at all is a separate question governed elsewhere in 247 CMR 8.00.
worked_examples.resolution: The reassignment takes the shift out of the ratio, because the exclusion in 247 CMR 8.06(3)(b) follows what the person is doing from moment to moment rather than the title on the schedule. The error the scenario invites is treating the exclusion as a fixed attribute of the cashier role, and a second error is treating a passing ratio as authorisation for the task, when the count and the scope of the task are separate checks.

worked_examples.scenario: A Schedule II delivery arrives at a Massachusetts pharmacy. The pharmacist asks a licensed pharmacy technician who is not certified to carry the sealed tote from the receiving bay to the safe, then to count the bottles and place them into the perpetual inventory bins. The pharmacy has written policies and procedures and the pharmacist has approved this individual in them. How far can the technician go?
steps: Start with 247 CMR 8.05(1): accountability for and security of Schedule II controlled substances is the direct responsibility of the pharmacist, and no approval shifts it.

Apply 247 CMR 8.05(2)(a). Under the supervision of a pharmacist a pharmacy technician may assist in the transporting of Schedule II controlled substances, which covers carrying the sealed tote to the safe.

Apply 247 CMR 8.05(2)(b). Assisting in the handling of Schedule II controlled substances is granted to the certified pharmacy technician, and counting the bottles into stock bins is handling rather than transporting.

Read the proviso in its place. The pharmacist's approval, evidenced by written policies and procedures to be followed in the pharmacy and available to the Board on request, is a condition attached to both grants; it is not itself a grant and it does not resize the one this individual holds.
worked_examples.resolution: The technician may carry the tote but may not count and shelve the stock, which needs a certified pharmacy technician or the pharmacist. The error the scenario invites is treating the approval and the written policies as the source of authority, when 247 CMR 8.05(2) has already sized the two grades differently and the documentation only conditions whatever grant the individual's grade already carries.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy takes in a hydrocodone-only extended release product that is not formulated in an abuse deterrent form. The Manager of Record proposes that only certified pharmacy technicians touch it, and that the pharmacist name them in the pharmacy's written policies and procedures, reasoning that the highest technician grade plus documented approval covers the product. Is that workable?
steps: Identify the governing sentence. 247 CMR 8.05(3) provides that a certified pharmacy technician, pharmacy technician, or pharmacy technician trainee may not handle any hydrocodone-only extended release medication that is not in an abuse deterrent form.
Notice that the prohibition names all three technician grades in one breath, so the certified grade is inside it rather than above it, and the proposal fails at its first step.

Notice next that the approval mechanism in 247 CMR 8.05(2) governs assistance with Schedule II controlled substances generally and attaches no qualification to 247 CMR 8.05(3), so the written policies cannot license what the later subsection forbids.

Identify who may. 247 CMR 8.05(3) expressly permits pharmacy interns under the direct supervision of a registered pharmacist to handle the product, which is the only affirmative permission the subsection contains.

Check the product description rather than the shelf. The prohibition reaches a hydrocodone-only extended release medication that is not in an abuse deterrent form, so an abuse deterrent formulation of the same drug falls outside it.
worked_examples.resolution: No technician grade may handle the product and the approval does not help; a pharmacist, or a pharmacy intern under the direct supervision of a registered pharmacist, must do it. The error the scenario invites is running a product-specific prohibition up the credential ladder, when 247 CMR 8.05(3) is drawn by product and formulation and names every technician grade at once.

worked_examples.scenario: The Manager of Record of a Massachusetts pharmacy is hospitalised without warning and will be away about two months. On the fourth day the pharmacy appoints an Interim Manager registered by the Board. No controlled substances inventory was performed before the absence, because nobody knew the absence was coming. The pharmacy treats the inventory as overtaken by events. Is anything still outstanding?
steps: Classify the absence. It is unplanned and likely to last 30 days or longer, so 247 CMR 9.23(5)(b) applies and the pharmacy had five days to appoint an Interim Manager registered by the Board. Day four is inside that period, so the appointment was timely.
Put the planned branch aside. 247 CMR 9.23(5)(a) requires appointment prior to a planned absence expected to last 30 days or longer, and these facts are not that case.

Read 247 CMR 9.23(5)(c) to its end. Its first sentence requires the Manager of Record to perform, prior to the absence, a controlled substances inventory signed by the Manager of Record and the Interim Manager, which these facts made impossible.

Apply the second sentence of the same provision: where the Manager of Record is unexpectedly not available, another registered pharmacist shall perform the controlled substances inventory. The duty is reassigned, not discharged by impossibility.

Check the outer threshold. 247 CMR 9.23(5)(d) requires an application for a change of Manager of Record where the Manager of Record is away from the position for 100 days or more, and about two months does not reach that.
worked_examples.resolution: The appointment was timely and no change-of-Manager application is triggered, but the controlled substances inventory is still owed and another registered pharmacist must perform it. The error the scenario invites is treating the unexpectedness that made the pre-absence inventory impossible as an excuse for it, when 247 CMR 9.23(5)(c) answers that case by naming a substitute performer.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy orders new staff badges. To keep them uniform it prints surname only on every badge, and it gives a pharmacy technician trainee a badge reading Pharmacy Technician because the trainee performs technician duties under the direct supervision of a pharmacist all shift. The Manager of Record asks whether either decision is a problem.
steps: Take the surname decision first. 247 CMR 8.02(6)(a), 247 CMR 8.03(4)(a) and 247 CMR 8.04(4)(a) each require the individual's first name on the tag, so a surname-only badge does not satisfy any of the three technician provisions.
Check the intern tier separately, because it is drafted differently: 247 CMR 8.01(14) calls for the intern's name and the words pharmacy intern rather than a first name and a title.

Take the title decision next. 247 CMR 8.03(4)(a) requires a pharmacy technician trainee to wear the title Pharmacy Technician Trainee, and each of the four provisions pairs one title with one credential.

Separate the credential from the assignment. That a trainee performs the duties of a pharmacy technician under direct supervision is a fact about the work; the tag states the credential the individual holds, which is the trainee licence.

Note what the tags are doing for the shift as a whole, since 247 CMR 8.06(3)(a) sorts the same four categories by credential, and a badge announcing the wrong tier misdescribes the very composition the ratio is calculated on.
worked_examples.resolution: Both decisions are wrong for the technician tiers: every pharmacy technician, trainee and certified pharmacy technician badge needs the individual's first name, and the trainee's badge must read Pharmacy Technician Trainee. An intern's badge is measured by 247 CMR 8.01(14) instead, which asks for the intern's name and the words pharmacy intern rather than a first name. The error the scenario invites is treating the name tag as a description of the job being performed, when each provision ties one displayed title to one credential held.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: One pharmacist may supervise a maximum of four support personnel only on one of three conditions. Name all three.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Under 247 CMR 8.06(3)(a)1: at least one of the four is a certified pharmacy technician and one is a pharmacy intern; or at least two of the support personnel are certified pharmacy technicians; or two of the support personnel are pharmacy interns.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What condition attaches to the three-person supervisory ratio?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Under 247 CMR 8.06(3)(a)2, at least one of the three support personnel must be a pharmacy intern or a certified pharmacy technician.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A cashier is excluded from the supervisory ratio ______ and ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Because the cashier does not fall within the definitions of a pharmacy intern, certified pharmacy technician, pharmacy technician or pharmacy technician trainee; and as long as the cashier is not supporting the pharmacist in any professional capacity. 247 CMR 8.06(3)(b) states both limbs.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which name tag provision does not confine the tag to the individual's first name?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 247 CMR 8.01(14), which calls for the intern's name and the words pharmacy intern. The three technician provisions each require the individual's first name and a stated title.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What title must a pharmacy technician trainee display, and on what does that depend?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Pharmacy Technician Trainee, with the individual's first name, under 247 CMR 8.03(4)(a). It depends on the credential held rather than on the duties assigned that shift.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 247 CMR 8.05(2), a pharmacy technician may assist in ______ and a certified pharmacy technician may assist in ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The transporting of Schedule II controlled substances; the transporting and handling of Schedule II controlled substances. Both are under the supervision of a pharmacist.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What must exist before either Schedule II grant in 247 CMR 8.05(2) operates, and where must it be available?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The pharmacist must have approved the individual to assist, evidenced by written policies and procedures to be followed in the pharmacy, which shall be made available to the Board on request.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a certified pharmacy technician may handle a hydrocodone-only extended release medication that is not in an abuse deterrent form if the pharmacist approves in writing.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. 247 CMR 8.05(3) names the certified pharmacy technician, the pharmacy technician and the pharmacy technician trainee together, and the approval mechanism in 247 CMR 8.05(2) does not qualify it.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who may handle a hydrocodone-only extended release medication that is not in an abuse deterrent form, and on what condition?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A pharmacy intern, under the direct supervision of a registered pharmacist, by the express terms of 247 CMR 8.05(3). The pharmacist retains accountability and security under 247 CMR 8.05(1).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the three items a Manager of Record must make available to the Board on request under 247 CMR 8.06(1).
retrieval_prompts.answer: A list of currently employed certified pharmacy technicians, pharmacy technicians and pharmacy technician trainees; a written description of the duties delegated to them; and a written description of their scopes of responsibility.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which tier appears in the supervisory ratios but not in the 247 CMR 8.06(1) document set?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The pharmacy intern. 247 CMR 8.06(3)(a) counts interns, while 247 CMR 8.06(1) names only certified pharmacy technicians, pharmacy technicians and pharmacy technician trainees.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A Board inspector asks for the written description of delegated technician duties and the Manager of Record has never filed it. What is the position?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It must be produced now. 247 CMR 8.06(1) is a duty to make the documents available to the Board upon request, not a duty to file them in advance, so never having filed is not an answer.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A planned Manager of Record absence of 30 days or longer requires what, and by when?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Appointment of an Interim Manager who is registered by the Board, prior to the absence, under 247 CMR 9.23(5)(a). The five-day period belongs to the unplanned branch in 247 CMR 9.23(5)(b).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who performs the controlled substances inventory when the Manager of Record is unexpectedly not available?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Another registered pharmacist, under 247 CMR 9.23(5)(c). The duty is reassigned rather than excused.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What follows when a Manager of Record is away from the position for 100 days or more?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The pharmacy shall submit an application for a change of Manager of Record, under 247 CMR 9.23(5)(d).

quick_review.text: 247 CMR 8.06(3)(a) counts pharmacy interns, certified pharmacy technicians, pharmacy technicians and pharmacy technician trainees whom a pharmacist is utilizing to assist in filling prescriptions, and 247 CMR 8.06(3)(b) keeps anyone else out of the count only while that person gives the pharmacist no professional support.
A maximum of four support personnel requires one certified pharmacy technician plus one pharmacy intern, or two certified pharmacy technicians, or two pharmacy interns, under 247 CMR 8.06(3)(a)1.
A maximum of three support personnel requires at least one of the three to be a pharmacy intern or a certified pharmacy technician, under 247 CMR 8.06(3)(a)2.

247 CMR 8.06(3)(b) excludes sales clerks, messengers, delivery personnel, secretaries and other persons outside the four definitions, as long as they are not supporting the pharmacist in any professional capacity.

Each of the four tiers wears a tag stating one credential: pharmacy intern under 247 CMR 8.01(14), Pharmacy Technician under 8.02(6)(a), Pharmacy Technician Trainee under 8.03(4)(a), Certified Pharmacy Technician under 8.04(4)(a).
The three technician tag provisions call for the individual's first name; 247 CMR 8.01(14) calls for the intern's name and the words pharmacy intern.
247 CMR 8.05(1) leaves accountability for and security of Schedule II controlled substances with the pharmacist directly, whatever assistance is delegated.
Under 247 CMR 8.05(2) a pharmacy technician may assist in transporting Schedule II controlled substances and a certified pharmacy technician may assist in transporting and handling them.
Both Schedule II grants depend on the pharmacist's approval of the individual, evidenced by written policies and procedures made available to the Board on request under 247 CMR 8.05(2).

247 CMR 8.05(3) bars every technician grade from handling hydrocodone-only extended release medication that is not in an abuse deterrent form, and expressly permits pharmacy interns under the direct supervision of a registered pharmacist.

247 CMR 8.06(1) requires the Manager of Record, or an institutional Director of Pharmacy, to produce a personnel list, a delegated duties description and a scopes of responsibility description on Board request.

247 CMR 8.06(2) requires on-the-job training programs to comply with written pharmacy guidelines consistent with professional, ethical, and legal standards of proper pharmacy practice, with copies provided to the Board on request.
247 CMR 9.23(5) sets 30 days as the absence threshold, five days as the unplanned appointment deadline, and 100 days as the point at which a change of Manager of Record must be applied for.

The pre-absence controlled substances inventory is signed by the Manager of Record and the Interim Manager, and passes to another registered pharmacist where the Manager of Record is unexpectedly not available.

decision_logic.condition: A ratio question gives a roster and asks whether the pharmacist is over the limit.
decision_logic.action: Count the pharmacy interns, certified pharmacy technicians, pharmacy technicians and pharmacy technician trainees the pharmacist is utilizing to assist in filling prescriptions under 247 CMR 8.06(3)(a), and add anyone else who is supporting the pharmacist in any professional capacity, because 247 CMR 8.06(3)(b) excludes persons outside the four definitions only while they give no such support. Then test the composition conditions rather than the headcount.

decision_logic.condition: The roster contains four support personnel.
decision_logic.action: Run all three conditions in 247 CMR 8.06(3)(a)1 in turn: one certified pharmacy technician with one pharmacy intern; two certified pharmacy technicians; two pharmacy interns. If none is satisfied, the four-person ratio is unavailable.

decision_logic.condition: A non-credentialed employee such as a cashier, messenger, delivery person or secretary is on duty.
decision_logic.action: Ask what that person is actually doing. Under 247 CMR 8.06(3)(b) the exclusion holds only while the person is not supporting the pharmacist in any professional capacity, so re-test the count whenever the assignment changes.

decision_logic.condition: A question turns on what a badge should say.
decision_logic.action: Identify the tier the individual actually holds, remembering that the certified tier is the Board pharmacy technician licence plus current certification by a Board-approved certifying body, and read the matching provision: 247 CMR 8.01(14), 8.02(6)(a), 8.03(4)(a) or 8.04(4)(a). Do not reason from the duties being performed, and treat a lapsed certification as returning the individual to the pharmacy technician title.

decision_logic.condition: Support personnel are being assigned to Schedule II stock.
decision_logic.action: Ask first whether the task is transporting or handling, then match it to the grade: 247 CMR 8.05(2)(a) gives the pharmacy technician transporting, and 247 CMR 8.05(2)(b) gives the certified pharmacy technician transporting and handling.

decision_logic.condition: The facts stress that the pharmacist approved the individual and the pharmacy has written policies and procedures.
decision_logic.action: Treat that as the condition 247 CMR 8.05(2) attaches to both grants, and confirm the policies are available to the Board on request. Do not treat it as widening the grade's own authority.

decision_logic.condition: The product is a hydrocodone-only extended release medication.
decision_logic.action: Ask whether it is in an abuse deterrent form. If it is not, 247 CMR 8.05(3) bars every technician grade from handling it and permits a pharmacy intern under the direct supervision of a registered pharmacist.

decision_logic.condition: A Board inspector asks a Manager of Record for technician documentation that was never filed.
decision_logic.action: Apply 247 CMR 8.06(1) as a duty of production on request, and produce the personnel list, the delegated duties description and the scopes of responsibility description.

decision_logic.condition: A Manager of Record is going to be absent.
decision_logic.action: Ask whether the absence is planned or unplanned and whether it is expected or likely to last 30 days or longer, because 247 CMR 9.23(5)(a) requires appointment before a planned absence and 247 CMR 9.23(5)(b) allows five days after an unplanned one.

decision_logic.condition: The pre-absence controlled substances inventory was not performed because the absence began without warning.
decision_logic.action: Apply the second sentence of 247 CMR 9.23(5)(c): another registered pharmacist performs the inventory. Do not record the duty as excused.

decision_logic.condition: The absence has run long.
decision_logic.action: Measure it against 100 days, at which point 247 CMR 9.23(5)(d) requires the pharmacy to submit an application for a change of Manager of Record rather than to extend the interim arrangement.

exceptions.text: 247 CMR 8.06(3)(b) takes sales clerks, messengers, delivery personnel, secretaries and any other persons outside the four defined categories out of the supervisory ratio, conditional on their not supporting the pharmacist in any professional capacity.

247 CMR 8.05(3) expressly permits pharmacy interns under the direct supervision of a registered pharmacist to handle hydrocodone-only extended release medication that is not in an abuse deterrent formulation, which no technician grade may handle.
An abuse deterrent formulation removes a hydrocodone-only extended release product from the prohibition in 247 CMR 8.05(3), which is drawn by product rather than by credential.
In an institutional pharmacy the Director of Pharmacy stands in the place of the pharmacist Manager of Record for the production duties in 247 CMR 8.06(1).
Where the Manager of Record is unexpectedly not available, 247 CMR 9.23(5)(c) substitutes another registered pharmacist as the person who performs the controlled substances inventory.

timing_deadlines.event: A planned absence of the Manager of Record expected to last 30 days or longer
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Before the absence begins
timing_deadlines.consequence: The pharmacy must already have appointed an Interim Manager registered by the Board; the five-day allowance does not apply to a planned absence.

timing_deadlines.event: An unplanned absence of the Manager of Record likely to last 30 days or longer
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within five days
timing_deadlines.consequence: An Interim Manager registered by the Board must be appointed within that period.

timing_deadlines.event: The controlled substances inventory tied to a qualifying absence
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Prior to the absence
timing_deadlines.consequence: The Manager of Record performs it and it is signed by the Manager of Record and the Interim Manager; where the Manager of Record is unexpectedly unavailable another registered pharmacist performs it instead.

timing_deadlines.event: A Manager of Record away from the position for 100 days or more
timing_deadlines.timeframe: 100 days
timing_deadlines.consequence: The pharmacy shall submit an application for a change of Manager of Record.

timing_deadlines.event: A Board request for the personnel list, delegated duties description or scopes of responsibility description
timing_deadlines.timeframe: On request
timing_deadlines.consequence: The documents must be made available then; 247 CMR 8.06(1) imposes no advance filing, so an absence of prior filing is neither compliance nor a defence.

timing_deadlines.event: A Board request for the written guidelines governing an on-the-job training program
timing_deadlines.timeframe: On request
timing_deadlines.consequence: Copies must be provided under 247 CMR 8.06(2); the guidelines are formulated by the pharmacy rather than approved by the Board in advance.

timing_deadlines.event: A Board request for the written policies and procedures evidencing a Schedule II assistance approval
timing_deadlines.timeframe: On request
timing_deadlines.consequence: They must be made available under 247 CMR 8.05(2); without them the pharmacist's approval is not evidenced as the provision requires.

forms_records.text: A list of currently employed certified pharmacy technicians, pharmacy technicians and pharmacy technician trainees, held by the Manager of Record or institutional Director of Pharmacy for production on Board request under 247 CMR 8.06(1)(a).
A written description of the duties delegated to certified pharmacy technicians, pharmacy technicians and pharmacy technician trainees, under 247 CMR 8.06(1)(b).
A written description of the scopes of responsibility for those same three tiers, under 247 CMR 8.06(1)(c). Pharmacy interns are named in none of the three items.

Written guidelines formulated by the pharmacy for any on-the-job training program, consistent with professional, ethical, and legal standards of proper pharmacy practice, with copies provided to the Board on request under 247 CMR 8.06(2).

Written policies and procedures to be followed in the pharmacy that evidence the pharmacist's approval of a pharmacy technician or certified pharmacy technician to assist with Schedule II controlled substances, made available to the Board on request under 247 CMR 8.05(2).
A controlled substances inventory performed before a qualifying Manager of Record absence and signed by the Manager of Record and the Interim Manager, under 247 CMR 9.23(5)(c).

The name tag is the only item in this material displayed continuously rather than produced on request, and it is what lets an inspector or a patient read the credential composition of a shift off the floor.

role_duties.duty: Comply with the supervisory ratios in 247 CMR 8.06(3)(a) when utilizing pharmacy interns, certified pharmacy technicians, pharmacy technicians and pharmacy technician trainees to assist in filling prescriptions, and re-count whenever an excluded employee is drawn into professional support.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist responsible for Schedule II stock
role_duties.duty: Retain accountability for and security of Schedule II controlled substances directly under 247 CMR 8.05(1), approve any technician or certified technician who is to assist, and see that the approval is evidenced by written policies and procedures available to the Board on request.

Wear a tag showing the individual's first name and the title Certified Pharmacy Technician, assist in transporting and handling Schedule II controlled substances only under pharmacist supervision and approval, and handle no hydrocodone-only extended release medication that is not in an abuse deterrent form.

Wear a tag showing the individual's first name and the title Pharmacy Technician, and assist with Schedule II controlled substances only in transporting them, which is the extent of the grant in 247 CMR 8.05(2)(a) whatever the written approval says.

Wear a tag showing the individual's first name and the title Pharmacy Technician Trainee, and handle no hydrocodone-only extended release medication that is not in an abuse deterrent form, a prohibition 247 CMR 8.05(3) applies to this tier by name.

Wear a tag indicating the intern's name and the words pharmacy intern, and, where the task is a hydrocodone-only extended release medication that is not in an abuse deterrent form, act only under the direct supervision of a registered pharmacist.

Keep the 247 CMR 8.06(1) personnel list, delegated duties description and scopes of responsibility description ready for production on Board request, and see that any on-the-job training program complies with written pharmacy guidelines whose copies are provided on request.

role_duties.role: Director of Pharmacy in an institutional pharmacy
role_duties.duty: Carry the 247 CMR 8.06(1) production duties in the place of the pharmacist Manager of Record where the institutional pharmacy utilizes certified pharmacy technicians, pharmacy technicians or pharmacy technician trainees.

role_duties.role: Manager of Record facing a qualifying absence
role_duties.duty: Perform a controlled substances inventory prior to the absence and have it signed by the Manager of Record and the Interim Manager, under 247 CMR 9.23(5)(c).

Appoint a Board-registered Interim Manager before a planned qualifying absence or within five days of an unplanned one, and submit an application for a change of Manager of Record once the Manager of Record has been away from the position for 100 days or more.
Be registered by the Board before taking the appointment, and sign the pre-absence controlled substances inventory alongside the Manager of Record.

role_duties.role: Registered pharmacist standing in for an unavailable Manager of Record
role_duties.duty: Perform the controlled substances inventory where the Manager of Record is unexpectedly not available, under 247 CMR 9.23(5)(c).

role_duties.role: Sales clerk, messenger, delivery person or secretary
role_duties.duty: Stay outside the supervisory ratio only while giving the pharmacist no professional support; the exclusion in 247 CMR 8.06(3)(b) is lost the moment that changes.

common_traps.text: Reading a maximum of four support personnel as a headcount allowance. Each of the three routes to four in 247 CMR 8.06(3)(a)1 is a condition on credential composition, and a roster meeting none of them cannot claim the four-person ratio.

Treating one certified pharmacy technician as enough for four support personnel. The first route pairs a certified pharmacy technician with a pharmacy intern and the second asks for two certified pharmacy technicians; one alone satisfies neither.
Counting current licences instead of credentials. Four pharmacy technicians with current licences satisfy no condition in 247 CMR 8.06(3)(a)1, because currency is not what the conditions ask about.

Treating the 247 CMR 8.06(3)(b) exclusion as a fixed attribute of a job title. It is conditioned on the person not supporting the pharmacist in any professional capacity, so it can be lost mid-shift by a reassignment.

Letting a name tag describe the work rather than the credential. Each of 247 CMR 8.01(14), 8.02(6)(a), 8.03(4)(a) and 8.04(4)(a) ties one displayed title to one credential the individual holds; for the certified tier that credential is the Board pharmacy technician licence plus current certification by a Board-approved certifying body, not a separate Board licence.
Keeping the Certified Pharmacy Technician tag on after a certification lapses. Under 247 CMR 8.04(3) the individual must use the title pharmacy technician until the certification is current again.
Assuming every tag provision is drafted identically. The three technician provisions call for the individual's first name; 247 CMR 8.01(14) calls for the intern's name and the words pharmacy intern.

Collapsing the two technician grades into one Schedule II category. 247 CMR 8.05(2)(a) gives the pharmacy technician transporting, and only 247 CMR 8.05(2)(b) adds handling for the certified pharmacy technician.

Reading the pharmacist's written approval as the source of Schedule II authority. It is the condition attached to whatever grant the individual's grade already carries under 247 CMR 8.05(2), and it does not enlarge the narrower one.

Supposing that assistance with transporting or handling moves accountability. 247 CMR 8.05(1) keeps accountability for and security of Schedule II controlled substances with the pharmacist directly, and professional judgment is not delegated with the task.

Running the hydrocodone-only extended release prohibition up the credential ladder. 247 CMR 8.05(3) names the certified pharmacy technician, the pharmacy technician and the pharmacy technician trainee together and turns on the product's formulation.

Expecting the 247 CMR 8.06(1) documents to have been filed with the Board. The duty is to make them available on request, so having never filed them is neither the violation nor the defence a question may suggest.
Assuming the 247 CMR 8.06(1) documents cover everyone counted in the ratio. Pharmacy interns are counted under 247 CMR 8.06(3) but appear in none of the three items in 247 CMR 8.06(1).

Applying the five-day appointment period to a planned absence. 247 CMR 9.23(5)(a) requires the Interim Manager to be appointed prior to a planned absence expected to last 30 days or longer; the five days in 247 CMR 9.23(5)(b) belong to an unplanned absence.

Treating the pre-absence controlled substances inventory as excused when the absence begins without warning. 247 CMR 9.23(5)(c) answers that case by requiring another registered pharmacist to perform it.
Triggering a change-of-Manager application on the 30-day threshold. That threshold governs the interim appointment; the application follows an absence from the position of 100 days or more.

drug_examples.teaching_point: A Schedule II combination of hydrocodone and acetaminophen is not a hydrocodone-only extended release medication, so 247 CMR 8.05(3) does not reach it and the ordinary 247 CMR 8.05(2) allocation applies: a pharmacy technician may assist in transporting it and a certified pharmacy technician in transporting and handling it. The prohibition turns on the product description, not on the presence of hydrocodone.

sections.title: Massachusetts Compounding Operations: Licence Categories, Engineering Controls and Hazardous Drugs
sections.topic: Compounding / Licence categories, engineering controls and hazardous-drug handling
sections.subtopic: The sterile and complex non-sterile compounding licence gates in M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39F and 247 CMR 6.02, the application, inspection and renewal requirements in 247 CMR 6.06 and 6.07, the statutory significant-difference test in s. 39D, secondary engineering control approval and the compounding submission in 247 CMR 6.15(2) and (4), and hazardous-drug handling reached through 247 CMR 9.01(3)
learning_objectives: Sort a proposed preparation into the sterile, complex non-sterile or ordinary category using the definitions in M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D before asking which licence is needed.

State the licence or combination of licences 247 CMR 6.02 requires before a pharmacy may engage in sterile compounding or in complex non-sterile compounding, and say why a Drug Store Pharmacy licence alone does not suffice.
List what 247 CMR 6.06(1) and 6.07(1) each require in support of an application, and name the one item that differs between them.
Place the satisfactory Board inspection in 247 CMR 6.06(2) and 6.07(2) correctly against issuance and against renewal.
Apply the significant-difference test in M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D and explain why a price difference cannot satisfy it.
Identify the acts on a secondary engineering control that 247 CMR 6.15(2) puts behind Board approval, and name the three pharmacy types the paragraph reaches.
Assemble the 247 CMR 6.15(4) submission and distinguish its addressees from those of 247 CMR 6.15(2).
Explain how 247 CMR 9.01(3) makes hazardous-drug handling standards binding on a Massachusetts licensee, and why those obligations do not stop at the compounding step.

orientation.text: Every question in this area begins with a classification rather than with a licence. M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D defines sterile compounding as engaging in the compounding of a sterile drug preparation, and defines a sterile drug preparation as a compounded biologic, diagnostic, drug, nutrient or radiopharmaceutical which under chapter 797 of the USP or under cGMP shall be compounded using aseptic techniques, a description the statute illustrates with implants, injectables, parenteral nutrition solutions, irrigation solutions, inhalation solution, intravenous solutions and ophthalmic preparations. Complex non-sterile compounding is defined in parallel as engaging in the compounding of a complex non-sterile drug preparation, which the same section defines as a compounded drug preparation requiring special training, a special environment or special facilities or equipment, or the use of compounding techniques and procedures that may present an elevated risk to the compounder or the patient, as defined by the Board through regulation. Both categories are properties of the preparation. Neither is chosen by the pharmacy, and the licence a pharmacy already holds has no power to move a preparation out of one category and into another.

Once the category is fixed the licence gate follows, and it is stated twice, once in statute and once in regulation. M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39F(a) provides that a pharmacy shall not engage in sterile compounding, nor prescribe, ship, mail, sell, transfer or dispense sterile drug preparations in the commonwealth, unless it has obtained a licence from the Board under the sections the statute names; s. 39F(b) states the same prohibition for complex non-sterile compounding and complex non-sterile drug preparations. Read those verbs, because the prohibition is not confined to the act of compounding. The regulation is more precise about what must actually be held. Under 247 CMR 6.02(2) a pharmacy may not engage in any sterile compounding unless it holds a Drug Store Pharmacy license and a sterile compounding pharmacy license, or an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy license. Under 247 CMR 6.02(3) a pharmacy may not engage in any complex non-sterile compounding unless it holds a Drug Store Pharmacy license and a complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy license. The compounding licence is therefore additional rather than alternative, which is why an ordinary drug-store licence does not substitute for it.

The two application sections are near-twins, and the difference that decides questions is a single item. Under 247 CMR 6.06(1) a sterile compounding pharmacy applicant submits all documentation identified in 247 CMR 6.04(2), certified blueprints of the compounding area or areas depicting the location and identifying the ISO classification for each primary and secondary engineering control, a detailed HVAC design plan with a written description, and an attestation of intent to engage in compounding signed by the Manager of Record, the pharmacist in charge of sterile compounding as applicable, and the applicants. Under 247 CMR 6.07(1) the complex non-sterile applicant submits the same four categories of document, but its blueprints are certified blueprints of the dedicated compounding room including placement of containment hoods, with no ISO classification of engineering controls. The two sections then converge again. 247 CMR 6.06(2) and 6.07(2) each require the applicant to achieve a satisfactory Board inspection of the proposed pharmacy prior to the issuance of the original licence, so the inspection sits ahead of issuance and cannot be treated as something a pharmacy grows into. And 247 CMR 6.06(3)(a) and 6.07(3)(a) each expire the licence on December 31st of each year following the date of its issuance, which makes these annual licences rather than biennial ones.

The significant-difference test is easy to miss because it sits inside the statutory definition of compounding rather than in a provision of its own. M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D defines compounding as the preparation, mixing, assembling, packaging or labeling of one or more active ingredients with one or more other substances, by or under the supervision of a licensed pharmacist within a licensed pharmacy, to create a final drug preparation formulated in one of three ways. The first way is the patient-specific one: for use on or for a patient as a result of a practitioner's prescription order, based on the relationship between practitioner, patient and pharmacist in the course of routine professional practice, to meet the unique medical need of an individual patient by producing a significant difference between the compounded drug preparation and a comparable commercially available drug that is justified by a documented medical need as determined by the prescribing practitioner. The statute offers examples, including the removal of a dye for medical reasons, a change in strength, and a change in dosage, form or delivery mechanism, and then forecloses the tempting one by providing that a price difference shall not be a significant difference to justify compounding. Why the test carries weight is structural. Except as provided in that patient-specific limb, compounding shall not include the preparation of commercially available, federally approved drugs or drug preparations, so the documented medical need is the thing that lifts a general exclusion, and cost cannot do that work.

247 CMR 6.15 is one section doing two different jobs, and the boundary between them is where marks are lost. 247 CMR 6.15(1) is the general remodelling half: it reaches a Drug Store pharmacy alongside the compounding pharmacy types and governs an application for approval to remodel or to change the configuration or square footage of the pharmacy. That half, and the drawings that 247 CMR 6.15(3) calls for from an applicant, belong to the pharmacy change-filings material and are not taught here. 247 CMR 6.15(2) is the engineering-control half, and it is narrower in every dimension. It names three pharmacy types only, a sterile compounding pharmacy, a non-resident sterile compounding pharmacy and an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy. It requires each of them to apply to the Board for approval to remodel or to change the configuration or square footage of the pharmacy prior to moving, adding, modifying, removing or replacing any secondary engineering control, and it bars each of them from moving, adding, modifying, removing or replacing any secondary engineering control until it receives approval from the Board. Two consequences follow. There is no separate engineering-control application: the vehicle is the same remodelling application, and what 6.15(2) supplies is a second occasion for filing it and a second prohibition. And because replacing appears on the list of acts, a like-for-like swap that alters no configuration and no square footage is still inside the provision.

247 CMR 6.15(4) is the submission half, and its list of addressees is not the same list as 6.15(2)'s. It reaches a sterile compounding pharmacy, a complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy, an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy and a non-resident sterile compounding pharmacy, so a complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy that stands outside the secondary engineering control prohibition in 6.15(2) is nonetheless inside the submission requirement in 6.15(4), while a Drug Store pharmacy is outside both. Each of those four shall submit, in support of an application to remodel or to change the configuration or square footage of a pharmacy: certified blueprints depicting the compounding area or areas and the location and ISO classification of each primary and secondary engineering control, and the placement of containment hoods, as applicable; a containment strategy; an environmental monitoring plan, if applicable; a plan to re-certify primary and secondary engineering controls and containment hoods, if applicable; a continuity of care plan, if applicable; and any other information as required by the Board. Read the qualifiers instead of skipping them, because four of the six items are expressly conditioned as applicable or if applicable, so the list is a maximum shaped by the facility rather than six documents in every case. Note also that the certified blueprints called for by 6.15(4)(a) are the same instrument 247 CMR 6.06(1)(b) required in support of the original sterile compounding pharmacy licence.

Hazardous-drug handling reaches Massachusetts pharmacy law by incorporation rather than through a regulation of its own. 247 CMR 9.01(3) provides that, unless otherwise regulated by the Board, a licensee shall adhere to the most current standards established by each chapter of the United States Pharmacopeia. That single sentence is the whole mechanism: the hazardous-drug standards bind a Massachusetts licensee because 247 CMR 9.01(3) makes the current USP chapters binding, and the Board's own advisory on USP 800 in community pharmacies identifies the chapter that addresses hazardous drugs. Two consequences deserve fixing early. The first is that the hazardous framework is an overlay: a pharmacy compounding a hazardous drug must satisfy the sterile or non-sterile compounding framework applicable to the preparation and the current hazardous-drug handling standards at the same time, so hazard classification does not displace the compounding requirements and holding a compounding licence does not erase the hazardous-drug controls. The second is that the hazardous obligations are not confined to the act of compounding: they reach receipt, storage, compounding, dispensing, administration and disposal, which is why a pharmacy that only stores and dispenses intact manufacturer-packaged hazardous tablets is still inside the framework. What 247 CMR 9.01(3) does not supply is the technical detail. That detail lives in the current USP text rather than in the Massachusetts regulation, so a question turning on a specific containment level or a specific engineering-control specification is not answered out of 247 CMR 9.00 at all.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts sterile compounding pharmacy plans to swap an ageing cleanroom unit that everyone involved accepts is a secondary engineering control for an identical new one, in the same position and on the same footprint, over a single weekend. The director reasons that because neither the configuration nor the square footage of the pharmacy changes there is nothing to file, and that in any event the pharmacy will suspend all compounding while the work is done. What does 247 CMR 6.15 require?
steps: Do not start from whether the configuration changed. 247 CMR 6.15(2) is written as a list of acts performed on a secondary engineering control: moving, adding, modifying, removing or replacing.
Match the facts to that list. Swapping one unit for an identical one is replacing, which is expressly named, so an unchanged footprint does not carry the work outside the provision.

Check that the pharmacy is one of the three types 247 CMR 6.15(2) reaches: a sterile compounding pharmacy, a non-resident sterile compounding pharmacy or an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy. It is the first of the three.

Read the prohibition rather than hunting for a deadline. The pharmacy shall apply to the Board for approval prior to the act, and may not move, add, modify, remove or replace any secondary engineering control until it receives approval from the Board. No number of days appears anywhere in 6.15.

Assemble the submission from 247 CMR 6.15(4), which begins with certified blueprints depicting the compounding areas and the location and ISO classification of each primary and secondary engineering control and the placement of containment hoods, as applicable, and then adds a containment strategy, an environmental monitoring plan, a re-certification plan and a continuity of care plan, each as applicable.
Notice what suspending compounding does not achieve. Nothing in 247 CMR 6.15(2) conditions the approval requirement on whether compounding continues while the work is carried out.
worked_examples.resolution: The pharmacy must apply and wait for the Board's approval before the swap, and must support the application with the 247 CMR 6.15(4) items rather than with ordinary layout drawings. The error the scenario invites is reasoning from whether the configuration changed instead of from whether one of the five listed acts was performed on a secondary engineering control, with the offer to suspend compounding held out as a second false exit.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts pharmacy holds a Drug Store Pharmacy license and a complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy license. It proposes to begin preparing patient-specific ophthalmic preparations that will be compounded using aseptic technique. Its Manager of Record reasons that the pharmacy already holds a compounding licence, that every preparation will be patient-specific, and that any further application is a formality that can be completed once the service is running.
steps: Classify the preparation before looking at any licence. An ophthalmic preparation compounded using aseptic technique answers the M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D description of a sterile drug preparation, so the proposed activity is sterile compounding.

Apply the statutory prohibition. M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39F(a) bars a pharmacy from engaging in sterile compounding, and from dispensing sterile drug preparations in the commonwealth, without the licence the Board issues for it.

Read 247 CMR 6.02(2) for what must actually be held: a Drug Store Pharmacy license together with a sterile compounding pharmacy license, or an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy license. A complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy license is neither of those things.

Note that the licence category follows the preparation rather than the pharmacy. 247 CMR 6.02(3) licenses complex non-sterile compounding, and holding that licence says nothing about the sterile category.

Fix the sequence. 247 CMR 6.06(2) requires a satisfactory Board inspection of the proposed sterile compounding pharmacy prior to the issuance of an original sterile compounding pharmacy license, so the licence cannot trail the activity.
Set the patient-specific point aside. Patient-specific preparation is part of how M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D defines compounding; it is not a route around the licensure gate.
worked_examples.resolution: The pharmacy may not begin until it holds the sterile compounding pharmacy licence, and it cannot hold that licence until it has passed the satisfactory Board inspection that 247 CMR 6.06(2) places ahead of issuance. The error the scenario invites is treating a specialty licence as generic and patient-specific status as a waiver, when the category follows the preparation and the inspection gate sits before issuance rather than after it.

worked_examples.scenario: A prescriber telephones a Massachusetts pharmacy and asks it to compound an oral suspension of a drug that is already marketed as an approved oral suspension. Asked for the clinical reason, the prescriber explains that the patient's insurance will not cover the marketed product and the compounded version will be substantially cheaper, and offers to write that reason on the prescription so that the file shows a documented rationale.
steps: Start from the general exclusion rather than from the request. Under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D, and except as provided in the patient-specific limb, compounding shall not include the preparation of commercially available, federally approved drugs or drug preparations.

Read what the patient-specific limb actually asks for: a significant difference between the compounded drug preparation and a comparable commercially available drug, justified by a documented medical need, as determined by the prescribing practitioner.

Test the offered reason against the statutory illustrations, which include the removal of a dye for medical reasons, a change in strength, and a change in dosage, form or delivery mechanism. Insurance coverage and cost are not among them.
Apply the express exclusion. M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D provides that a price difference shall not be a significant difference to justify compounding.
Notice that writing the reason down does not repair it. What the statute requires to be documented is a medical need, so recording a financial one documents the wrong thing.
worked_examples.resolution: The request as stated does not support compounding, because the only difference offered is price and s. 39D excludes a price difference from the significant difference by name. The error the scenario invites is treating the prescriber's determination plus a written note as sufficient in themselves, when the statute requires the difference to be justified by a documented medical need.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts drug store pharmacy that holds no compounding licence of any kind begins stocking a manufacturer-packaged oral tablet identified as a hazardous drug. It will receive the tablets, store them, dispense them intact and dispose of the stock that expires, and it will not manipulate them in any way. The Manager of Record concludes that because the pharmacy does no compounding, and because the pharmacy licensure regulations say nothing about hazardous drugs, nothing further is required.
steps: Confirm the half of the reasoning that is sound. With no compounding, neither the sterile framework nor the complex non-sterile framework is engaged, and neither licence gate arises.

Find where the hazardous obligation actually originates. 247 CMR 9.01(3) provides that, unless otherwise regulated by the Board, a licensee shall adhere to the most current standards established by each chapter of the United States Pharmacopeia, and that incorporation is what makes the hazardous-drug standards binding on this pharmacy.

Take the breadth of what is incorporated seriously. Hazardous-drug handling reaches receipt, storage, compounding, dispensing, administration and disposal, so the compounding step is one stage among several rather than the trigger.
Reject the inference drawn from the wrong regulation. The obligation does not travel through the pharmacy licensure sections, so their silence about hazardous drugs creates no exemption.
Map the framework onto the operations this pharmacy actually performs: receiving, storing, dispensing and disposing of the intact product.
worked_examples.resolution: The pharmacy sits inside the hazardous-drug handling framework for the receipt, storage, dispensing and disposal it performs, even though it compounds nothing and holds no compounding licence. The error the scenario invites is reading hazardous-drug controls as a compounding topic and treating the licensure regulation's silence as permission.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 247 CMR 6.02(2) a pharmacy may engage in sterile compounding only if it holds ______ together with ______, or alternatively ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: A Drug Store Pharmacy license; a sterile compounding pharmacy license; an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy license.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which licence combination does 247 CMR 6.02(3) require before a pharmacy may engage in any complex non-sterile compounding?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A Drug Store Pharmacy license and a complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy license. No institutional alternative is stated for this category.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which acts, besides compounding itself, does M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39F(a) forbid a pharmacy to perform on sterile drug preparations in the commonwealth without the required licence?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Prescribing, shipping, mailing, selling, transferring and dispensing them.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What single item separates the blueprints required by 247 CMR 6.06(1)(b) from those required by 247 CMR 6.07(1)(b)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The sterile application's certified blueprints depict the compounding areas and identify the ISO classification for each primary and secondary engineering control; the complex non-sterile application's certified blueprints are of the dedicated compounding room and show placement of containment hoods.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: the satisfactory Board inspection in 247 CMR 6.06(2) is a condition of renewing a sterile compounding pharmacy licence.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. It is required prior to the issuance of an original sterile compounding pharmacy license. Renewal under 247 CMR 6.06(3)(b) instead carries copies of all reports or correspondence pertaining to inspections by any state or federal agency, or any entity inspecting on behalf of one, occurring within the pending licensing period.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: On what date does a sterile compounding pharmacy licence or a complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy licence expire?
retrieval_prompts.answer: December 31st of each year following the date of its issuance, under 247 CMR 6.06(3)(a) and 6.07(3)(a). Both are annual licences.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the five acts on a secondary engineering control that 247 CMR 6.15(2) places behind Board approval.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Moving, adding, modifying, removing and replacing.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which three pharmacy types does 247 CMR 6.15(2) name, and which type appears in 247 CMR 6.15(4) but not in 6.15(2)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A sterile compounding pharmacy, a non-resident sterile compounding pharmacy and an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy. A complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy appears in 6.15(4) but not in 6.15(2).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: List the items 247 CMR 6.15(4) requires in support of an application to remodel or to change the configuration or square footage of a pharmacy.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Certified blueprints depicting the compounding areas and the location and ISO classification of each primary and secondary engineering control and the placement of containment hoods, as applicable; a containment strategy; an environmental monitoring plan, if applicable; a plan to re-certify primary and secondary engineering controls and containment hoods, if applicable; a continuity of care plan, if applicable; and any other information as required by the Board.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Complete the statutory phrase: under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D a ______ difference shall not be a significant difference to justify compounding.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Price.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: In the patient-specific limb of the M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D compounding definition, what must justify the significant difference, and who determines it?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A documented medical need, as determined by the prescribing practitioner.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which provision makes current USP standards binding on a Massachusetts pharmacy licensee, and on what condition?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 247 CMR 9.01(3): unless otherwise regulated by the Board, a licensee shall adhere to the most current standards established by each chapter of the United States Pharmacopeia.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a pharmacy holding the correct compounding licence has by that fact satisfied its hazardous-drug obligations for a hazardous preparation.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. The two frameworks stack. The pharmacy must satisfy the applicable sterile or non-sterile compounding framework and the current hazardous-drug handling standards together, and neither displaces the other.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name activities other than compounding that current hazardous-drug handling standards reach.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Receipt, storage, dispensing, administration and disposal.

quick_review.text: Classification precedes licensure: M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D fixes the sterile and complex non-sterile categories by the nature of the preparation, not by what the pharmacy already holds.
247 CMR 6.02(2): sterile compounding requires a Drug Store Pharmacy license and a sterile compounding pharmacy license, or an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy license.
247 CMR 6.02(3): complex non-sterile compounding requires a Drug Store Pharmacy license and a complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy license.

M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39F(a) and (b) forbid more than compounding without the licence; they also forbid prescribing, shipping, mailing, selling, transferring and dispensing the corresponding preparations in the commonwealth.

The sterile application's certified blueprints carry ISO classification for each primary and secondary engineering control under 247 CMR 6.06(1)(b); the complex non-sterile application's show the dedicated compounding room and containment hood placement under 247 CMR 6.07(1)(b).
A satisfactory Board inspection precedes issuance of the original licence in both categories, under 247 CMR 6.06(2) and 6.07(2).

Both compounding licences expire on December 31st of each year following issuance, and renewal carries copies of all reports and correspondence about state or federal inspections occurring within the pending licensing period.

A price difference shall not be a significant difference to justify compounding; the difference must be justified by a documented medical need as determined by the prescribing practitioner, under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D.

247 CMR 6.15(2) puts moving, adding, modifying, removing and replacing any secondary engineering control behind Board approval for a sterile compounding, non-resident sterile compounding or institutional sterile compounding pharmacy, and states no day count.

247 CMR 6.15(4) adds certified blueprints with ISO classification and containment hood placement, a containment strategy, an environmental monitoring plan, a re-certification plan, a continuity of care plan and any other information the Board requires, for four pharmacy types including a complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy.

247 CMR 9.01(3) is the doorway for hazardous drugs: unless otherwise regulated by the Board, a licensee shall adhere to the most current standards established by each chapter of the United States Pharmacopeia.
Hazardous status is an overlay. The applicable compounding framework and the hazardous-drug standards apply together, and neither substitutes for the other.
Hazardous-drug obligations reach receipt, storage, compounding, dispensing, administration and disposal, so they can attach where no compounding occurs at all.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacy proposes a new preparation and asks which licence it needs.
decision_logic.action: Classify the preparation first under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D as a sterile drug preparation, a complex non-sterile drug preparation, or neither, and only then read 247 CMR 6.02 for the licence that category requires.

decision_logic.condition: The preparation answers the statutory description of a sterile drug preparation.
decision_logic.action: Require a Drug Store Pharmacy license together with a sterile compounding pharmacy license, or an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy license, before any sterile compounding begins, and expect the satisfactory Board inspection in 247 CMR 6.06(2) ahead of issuance of the original licence.

decision_logic.condition: The preparation answers the statutory description of a complex non-sterile drug preparation.
decision_logic.action: Require a Drug Store Pharmacy license together with a complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy license under 247 CMR 6.02(3), and expect the satisfactory Board inspection in 247 CMR 6.07(2) ahead of issuance of the original licence.

decision_logic.condition: A commercially available approved product would serve the patient and compounding is nonetheless requested.
decision_logic.action: Ask what significant difference the compounded preparation produces for that patient, whether it is justified by a documented medical need, and whether the prescribing practitioner determined it. If the only difference offered is price, M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D forecloses it.

decision_logic.condition: A facility change is proposed at a compounding pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Ask two separate questions. Will any secondary engineering control be moved, added, modified, removed or replaced, which engages 247 CMR 6.15(2); and is the pharmacy one of the four types named in 247 CMR 6.15(4), which fixes what the submission must contain.

decision_logic.condition: A secondary engineering control will be touched at a sterile compounding, non-resident sterile compounding or institutional sterile compounding pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Apply to the Board for approval before the act and do not perform it until approval is received. Do not look for a day count, because 247 CMR 6.15(2) states none.

decision_logic.condition: The drug being compounded is hazardous.
decision_logic.action: Run both frameworks in parallel: the sterile or non-sterile compounding framework that fits the preparation, and the current hazardous-drug handling standards engaged by 247 CMR 9.01(3).

decision_logic.condition: A hazardous drug is present but nothing will be compounded.
decision_logic.action: Apply the current hazardous-drug handling standards to the operations actually performed, including receipt, storage, dispensing and disposal, and do not look to the compounding licensure sections for the answer.

ma_vs_federal.text: M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39F(d) makes a federal determination operate directly as a Massachusetts prohibition: a pharmacy shall not compound any drug preparations banned by the federal Food and Drug Administration because of safety concerns.

M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39F(c) routes an entity out of the pharmacy framework and into the federal one where it intends to compound and distribute a sterile drug preparation or a complex non-sterile drug in volumes inconsistent with routinely observed volume patterns associated with patient-specific prescriptions, or in the absence of accountability documentation. Such an entity shall adhere to the most current cGMP standards and shall register either as a producer of drugs with the federal Food and Drug Administration or as an outsourcing facility with that agency and with the Board, before engaging in any sterile or complex non-sterile compounding.

Federal approval status frames the Massachusetts definition of compounding: except in the patient-specific limb, M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D provides that compounding shall not include the preparation of commercially available, federally approved drugs or drug preparations.

The compounding-licence renewal submission is not limited to Board inspections. Under 247 CMR 6.06(3)(b) and 6.07(3)(b) it reaches all reports or correspondence pertaining to inspections by any state or federal agency, or any entity inspecting on behalf of a state or federal agency, occurring within the pending licensing period.

exceptions.text: The general exclusion of commercially available, federally approved drugs from the M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D definition of compounding is lifted only by the patient-specific limb, and only where the significant difference is justified by a documented medical need as determined by the prescribing practitioner.

247 CMR 6.02(2) offers an alternative rather than a single route: an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy license stands in place of the Drug Store Pharmacy licence and sterile compounding pharmacy licence pair. 247 CMR 6.02(3) states no comparable alternative for complex non-sterile compounding.

Four of the six items in the 247 CMR 6.15(4) submission are conditional on their own terms: the certified blueprints show containment hood placement as applicable, and the environmental monitoring plan, the re-certification plan and the continuity of care plan are each required if applicable.

247 CMR 6.15(2) names a sterile compounding pharmacy, a non-resident sterile compounding pharmacy and an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy only. A complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy and a Drug Store pharmacy fall outside its secondary engineering control prohibition, although a complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy is inside the 247 CMR 6.15(4) submission.
247 CMR 9.01(3) binds the licensee to the most current USP standards only unless otherwise regulated by the Board, so a Board regulation addressing the same subject displaces the compendial standard.

timing_deadlines.event: Expiry of a sterile compounding pharmacy license
timing_deadlines.timeframe: December 31st of each year following the date of its issuance
timing_deadlines.consequence: 247 CMR 6.06(3)(a) makes this an annual licence; it does not run on the biennial personal-registration cycle.

timing_deadlines.event: Expiry of a complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy license
timing_deadlines.timeframe: December 31st of each year following the date of its issuance
timing_deadlines.consequence: 247 CMR 6.07(3)(a) sets the same annual expiry as the sterile compounding licence.

timing_deadlines.event: Satisfactory Board inspection of a proposed compounding pharmacy
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Prior to the issuance of the original licence
timing_deadlines.consequence: 247 CMR 6.06(2) and 6.07(2) place the inspection ahead of issuance, so an activity cannot be begun and regularised afterwards.

timing_deadlines.event: Moving, adding, modifying, removing or replacing a secondary engineering control
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Prior to the act; 247 CMR 6.15(2) states no number of days
timing_deadlines.consequence: The pharmacy may not perform the act until it receives approval from the Board, so the controlling constraint is the prohibition rather than a deadline.

timing_deadlines.event: Inspection reports filed with a compounding licence renewal
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Inspections occurring within the pending licensing period
timing_deadlines.consequence: 247 CMR 6.06(3)(b) and 6.07(3)(b) require copies of all reports or correspondence pertaining to inspections by any state or federal agency, or any entity inspecting on behalf of one, in that period.

forms_records.text: The sterile compounding pharmacy application under 247 CMR 6.06(1) carries all documentation identified in 247 CMR 6.04(2), certified blueprints of the compounding areas depicting the location and ISO classification of each primary and secondary engineering control, a detailed HVAC design plan and written description, and an attestation of intent to engage in compounding signed by the Manager of Record, the pharmacist in charge of sterile compounding as applicable, and the applicants.

The complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy application under 247 CMR 6.07(1) carries all documentation identified in 247 CMR 6.04(2), certified blueprints of the dedicated compounding room including placement of containment hoods, a detailed HVAC design plan and written description, and an attestation of intent to engage in compounding signed by the Manager of Record, the pharmacist in charge of complex non-sterile compounding as applicable, and the applicants.

The 247 CMR 6.15(4) submission consists of certified blueprints depicting the compounding areas and the location and ISO classification of each primary and secondary engineering control and the placement of containment hoods as applicable, a containment strategy, an environmental monitoring plan if applicable, a plan to re-certify primary and secondary engineering controls and containment hoods if applicable, a continuity of care plan if applicable, and any other information as required by the Board.

A compounding licence renewal under 247 CMR 6.06(3)(b) or 6.07(3)(b) carries copies of all reports or correspondence pertaining to all inspections by any state or federal agency, or any entity inspecting on behalf of a state or federal agency, occurring within the pending licensing period.

The medical need justifying a significant difference under M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D must be documented, and the prescribing practitioner is the one who determines it; a note recording a financial reason does not satisfy the requirement.

247 CMR 9.01(3) creates no Massachusetts hazardous-drug form or record of its own. What it requires is adherence to the most current USP standards, so the documentation expectations sit in that compendial text rather than in 247 CMR 9.00.

role_duties.role: Pharmacy proposing to begin sterile compounding
role_duties.duty: Hold a Drug Store Pharmacy license and a sterile compounding pharmacy license, or an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy license, before engaging in any sterile compounding, and pass the satisfactory Board inspection that 247 CMR 6.06(2) places ahead of issuance of the original licence.

role_duties.role: Pharmacy proposing to begin complex non-sterile compounding
role_duties.duty: Hold a Drug Store Pharmacy license and a complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy license before engaging in any complex non-sterile compounding, and pass the satisfactory Board inspection that 247 CMR 6.07(2) places ahead of issuance of the original licence.

Sign the attestation of intent to engage in compounding required by 247 CMR 6.06(1)(d) and 6.07(1)(d), alongside the pharmacist in charge of the relevant compounding category as applicable and the applicants.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist in charge of sterile compounding
role_duties.duty: Sign, as applicable under 247 CMR 6.06(1)(d), the attestation of intent to engage in compounding submitted in support of the sterile compounding pharmacy application.

role_duties.role: Sterile, non-resident sterile or institutional sterile compounding pharmacy
role_duties.duty: Apply to the Board for approval before moving, adding, modifying, removing or replacing any secondary engineering control, and refrain from the act until approval is received.
Determine the significant difference between the compounded preparation and a comparable commercially available drug, and rest that determination on a documented medical need rather than on price.

Satisfy the sterile or non-sterile compounding framework applicable to the preparation and the current hazardous-drug handling standards at the same time, treating neither as a substitute for the other.

role_duties.role: Any Massachusetts pharmacy licensee handling a hazardous drug
role_duties.duty: Adhere to the current hazardous-drug handling standards across receipt, storage, dispensing, administration and disposal, whether or not the pharmacy compounds anything.

common_traps.text: Reasoning from whether the configuration or square footage changed rather than from whether one of the five acts in 247 CMR 6.15(2) was performed on a secondary engineering control. Replacing is on the list, so a like-for-like swap sits inside the provision.
Assuming the addressee lists in 247 CMR 6.15(2) and 6.15(4) are the same. A complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy is named in (4) and not in (2), and a Drug Store pharmacy is named in neither.

Filing ordinary layout drawings for an engineering-control change. 247 CMR 6.15(4)(a) calls for certified blueprints depicting the compounding areas and the location and ISO classification of each primary and secondary engineering control.

Treating a compounding licence as generic. The licence category follows the preparation, so a complex non-sterile compounding pharmacy license does not reach sterile compounding, and a sterile compounding pharmacy license does not reach complex non-sterile compounding.

Reading non-sterile as a synonym for simple. The complex non-sterile category turns on special training, a special environment or special facilities or equipment, or techniques and procedures presenting an elevated risk to the compounder or the patient.

Treating patient-specific preparation as a waiver of the licensure gate. Patient-specific formulation is part of how M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D defines compounding; it says nothing about which licence the activity requires.

Accepting a documented reason as a documented medical need. M.G.L. c. 112, s. 39D requires the significant difference to be justified by a documented medical need, and it excludes a price difference by name.

Expecting the satisfactory inspection to be a renewal condition. 247 CMR 6.06(2) and 6.07(2) place it before issuance of the original licence, and what renewal carries instead is the inspection-report submission.
Reading hazardous-drug controls as a compounding topic. They reach receipt, storage, dispensing, administration and disposal, so a pharmacy that compounds nothing can still be inside the framework.

Treating the compounding framework and the hazardous-drug standards as alternatives. Hazard classification does not displace the sterile or non-sterile requirements, and satisfying those requirements does not erase the hazardous-drug controls.
