sections.title: The Collaborative Practice Agreement as a Document
sections.topic: Collaborative practice / The collaborative practice agreement itself
sections.subtopic: Valid constitution and biennial currency under M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(a) and 247 CMR 16.04(4); what counts as written under 243 CMR 2.12(1); the delegation terms required by 247 CMR 16.04(3); the copy-and-original custody split in 247 CMR 16.04(6) and 243 CMR 2.12; the two termination duties in 247 CMR 16.04(5); and the notification and continuing education evidence duties in 247 CMR 16.02(2) and (3)
learning_objectives: State the four constitutive elements of a collaborative practice agreement in M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(a) and say which of them the supervising physician's own scope of practice controls.
Separate valid constitution from continuing currency, and apply the biennial review and renewal requirement to an agreement whose formation was faultless.
Decide whether a paper or an electronic collaborative document satisfies the definition of written in 243 CMR 2.12(1), and name the conditions that attach only to the electronic route.
List the four delegation elements 247 CMR 16.04(3) requires an agreement to specify, and explain why an agreement's silence on delegation is not permission.
Allocate the agreement, the patient referral and the patient consent between the authorized pharmacist and the supervising physician, and say where each copy sits and who may call for it.
Distinguish the pre-termination duty to arrange an uninterrupted continuation of therapy from the duty to inform the patient in writing at the ending, and identify who owes each.
Apply the duty to notify each supervising physician of discipline or a practice restriction, including where the discipline is by consent agreement.
Compute the retention period for evidence of collaborative practice continuing education and identify the date the clock runs from.

orientation.text: A Massachusetts collaborative practice agreement is a document before it is a working arrangement, and most of what is tested here is decided by reading the instrument rather than by asking what the pharmacist did at the counter. M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(a) defines a collaborative practice agreement as a written and signed agreement between a pharmacist with training and experience relevant to the scope of the collaborative practice and a supervising physician, that defines the collaborative practice in which the pharmacist and supervising physician propose to engage. Four elements travel with that definition and each one is capable of failing on its own. The agreement must be written. It must be signed. Its parties are a pharmacist whose training and experience are relevant to the scope of the collaborative practice, and a supervising physician. And the collaborative practice the document defines must be within the scope of the supervising physician's practice, so the agreement cannot enlarge what the pharmacist co-manages past the boundary of what the physician's own practice covers. The Board of Registration in Pharmacy restates the same definition in its own regulations at 247 CMR 16.04(1). An oral understanding between two willing professionals is not a collaborative practice agreement, and neither is a signed document that reaches into territory the supervising physician does not practise in.

Valid constitution and current standing are two separate tests, and an agreement can pass the first and fail the second. The same statutory definition provides that each collaborative practice agreement shall be subject to review and renewal on a biennial basis, and 247 CMR 16.04(4), headed Biennial Renewal, puts the same duty in operational terms: a collaborative practice agreement must be reviewed and renewed by the authorized pharmacist and supervising physician or physicians at least every two years. Two details in that sentence carry weight. The duty sits on the parties themselves rather than on a board, so nobody will prompt them; and the two-year figure is a ceiling on the interval rather than a schedule, so reviewing sooner is compliance and letting the interval run longer is not. The definition also carries one content requirement of its own: a collaborative practice agreement shall include individually developed guidelines for any prescriptive practice of the pharmacist. The practical consequence is that a set of facts describing a faultlessly formed agreement is not finished until the date of the last review has been located. An agreement made correctly twenty-six months ago and never reviewed since is no longer current, whatever its contents say.

Because so much of this regime turns on documents, the regulations define what written means, and the definition is not the intuitive one. Under 243 CMR 2.12(1), all references to written regarding collaborative practice agreement referrals, consents and any other documents related to a collaborative practice agreement shall be, if paper based, written in ink, indelible pencil or any other means; or transmitted electronically in a format that maintains patient confidentiality and can be read and stored in a retrievable and readable form. Read the two routes side by side and the asymmetry is deliberate. The paper route is extremely permissive, and indelible pencil is named in the text itself, so a document that looks informal is not thereby defective. The electronic route is the conditioned one: it must maintain patient confidentiality, and the format must be capable of being read and of being stored in a retrievable and readable form. The same paragraph adds that collaborative practice agreements and related referrals, consents and other documentation may be transmitted electronically with the electronic signature or signatures without alteration of the information, provided the electronic transmission is in accordance with the requirements of M.G.L. c. 94C, § 23(g), 105 CMR 721.00, and 247 CMR 9.01(19) and 9.07(1)(a). An emailed image that the receiving system cannot store or retrieve in readable form fails, and the fact that it arrived electronically is what put it at risk rather than what saved it.

The agreement must also settle in advance who else may do the work. 247 CMR 16.04(3), headed Duties, requires four separate statements, and it is easiest to keep them as two pairs. First, the agreement shall specify those duties of the authorized pharmacist that may be delegated to other appropriately trained and authorized staff, and those duties under the agreement that shall not be delegated. Second, the agreement shall specify when and how an authorized pharmacist may delegate duties under the agreement, and the duration and scope of the delegation. An agreement that names three delegable duties and two non-delegable ones has satisfied only the first pair. The consequence of the drafting is that silence in the agreement is not permission: where the instrument says nothing about delegation there is no delegation power to exercise, and the competence or certification of the staff member who would receive the duty does not supply one. The paragraph closes by preserving the ordinary scope rules, providing that pharmacy interns and pharmacy technician duties providing support to an authorized pharmacist acting under a collaborative practice agreement must be performed in accordance with 247 CMR 8.01 for pharmacy interns and 8.02 through 8.06 for pharmacy technicians. Collaborative practice does not displace those rules; it sits on top of them.

Custody of the finished document is split, and the split is not a matter the two professionals may allocate between themselves. Under 247 CMR 16.04(6), headed Agreement to Be Filed in Primary Practice Setting, an authorized pharmacist must maintain a copy of the current collaborative practice agreement, including copies of the current patient referral and patient consent, in the primary practice setting, readily retrievable at the request of the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and the Board of Registration in Medicine. Four things in that sentence are separately examinable: the pharmacist holds a copy and not the original; the copy must be of the current agreement; the referral and the consent travel with it, so the agreement alone is not the whole file; and the retrievability runs to two boards, not one. The word filed in the heading means filed in the practice setting, not filed with a board, and nothing in the paragraph makes board filing a condition of acting under the agreement. The other half of the split runs the other way: in accordance with 243 CMR 2.12, Collaborative Drug Therapy Management (CDTM) with Authorized Pharmacists, the supervising physician must maintain the original of the current agreement, including the original current patient referral and patient consent, in the patient's medical record in the custody of the supervising physician. A physician who hands the original to the pharmacist for safekeeping has not tidied the file; the physician has emptied a record the physician is required to hold.

Ending an agreement carries two duties, and they differ in timing, in content and in audience. 247 CMR 16.04(5), headed Termination, provides first that prior to termination or non-renewal of a collaborative drug therapy management agreement, an authorized pharmacist and supervising physician shall arrange for an uninterrupted continuation of the patient's drug therapy, in accordance with the terms of the agreement. It provides second that when an agreement is not renewed or collaborative drug therapy management is otherwise terminated, an authorized pharmacist and supervising physician shall inform the patient in writing of the termination and of the procedures in place for the continuation of the patient's drug therapy, again in accordance with the terms of the agreement. The first duty is owed before the ending and is about the therapy; the second is owed at the ending and is about telling the patient, in writing, both that it has ended and what the arrangements now are. Both are owed jointly by the pharmacist and the supervising physician, and both are measured against the terms the parties themselves wrote, which is one more reason the agreement is the document to read first. A plan that consists only of a letter sent after the lapse answers the second duty and misses the first entirely.

Two further paper duties attach to the authorized pharmacist while an agreement is on foot, and both are easy to miss because neither is triggered by anything happening to the agreement. Under 247 CMR 16.02(3), whenever an authorized pharmacist participating in collaborative drug therapy management is disciplined by the Board, whether by agreement or Board order, or is otherwise subject to any practice restrictions, the pharmacist must provide written notification of that discipline or practice restriction to each supervising physician. Three points do the work there. Resolution by consent agreement counts as discipline just as a Board order does, so a matter settled without a hearing still triggers the duty. The notice runs to each supervising physician, so a pharmacist working under several agreements owes several notices rather than one. And a practice restriction imposed outside formal discipline is enough on its own. Under 247 CMR 16.02(2), the same pharmacist must maintain evidence of completion of required continuing education for at least two years after the date of the current collaborative practice agreement. The clock is the striking feature: it runs from the date of the current agreement, not from the date the course was completed and not from the pharmacist's registration renewal, so old coursework is released by a new agreement date rather than by the passage of time. What is being retained is evidence of the continuing education required for participation, which under 247 CMR 16.02(1)(e) is at least five additional contact hours of Board-approved continuing education in each year of the term of the agreement, addressing areas of practice generally related to the particular collaborative practice agreement.

Three neighbouring subjects are deliberately left outside this section, and knowing where the edges are is part of answering cleanly. The first is what collaborative drug therapy management is and who may do it at all: the statutory definition of the practice, the pharmacist qualification list, the approved practice settings and the circumstances in which a supervising physician becomes ineligible are treated separately, and this section assumes rather than establishes that the two parties are eligible. The second is prescribing: what an authorized pharmacist may initiate, modify, discontinue or extend, and on what registration, is a separate regime, and this section touches prescriptive practice only to record that the statutory definition requires individually developed guidelines for it. The third is the community pharmacy or retail drug business setting, which carries its own patient referral, consent, age, vaccine and prescribing conditions and is treated on its own. One further limit should be stated plainly rather than left to inference: this section does not set out to inventory every clause a collaborative practice agreement must contain. It teaches the agreement terms carried by the rules it depends on, and silence here about any other clause is not a statement that no other clause is required.

worked_examples.scenario: A collaborative practice agreement was written, signed and within the supervising physician's scope when it was made twenty-six months ago, and it contains individually developed prescriptive guidelines. Neither party has reviewed it since. The pharmacist proposes to keep co-managing referred patients under it while a review is scheduled, on the footing that nothing about the arrangement has changed. Is she right?
steps: Run the constitutive elements first: M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(a) requires a written and signed agreement between a qualifying pharmacist and a supervising physician, defining a collaborative practice within the scope of the physician's practice. All of those are satisfied on these facts.

Then read the next sentence of the same definition, which is a continuing condition rather than a formation requirement: each collaborative practice agreement shall be subject to review and renewal on a biennial basis.

Confirm the operational statement of the same duty at 247 CMR 16.04(4): a collaborative practice agreement must be reviewed and renewed by the authorized pharmacist and supervising physician or physicians at least every two years.
Measure the interval. Twenty-six months is more than two years, so the review and renewal fell due at some point before month twenty-seven and has not happened.
Note who carries the duty. It sits on the pharmacist and the physician themselves, so no board notice was going to arrive, and a review that is merely scheduled is not a review that has been done.
worked_examples.resolution: The agreement is out of currency, and a pending review does not preserve it. The error the scenario invites is to run the formation checklist, find every element satisfied, and never ask when the instrument was last reviewed and renewed.

worked_examples.scenario: An authorized pharmacist holds two patient referrals. One was completed by the supervising physician in indelible pencil on a paper form. The other arrived by email as a flattened image that the pharmacy system can display once but can neither store nor retrieve afterwards in readable form. The pharmacist assumes the emailed one is the safer of the two because it is electronic and time-stamped. How should each be assessed?
steps: Start from the definition rather than from intuition: 243 CMR 2.12(1) says what written means for collaborative practice agreement referrals, consents and other related documents.

Apply the paper limb. A paper-based document satisfies the requirement if it is written in ink, indelible pencil or any other means, and indelible pencil is named in the regulation itself, so the pencil referral passes.

Apply the electronic limb, which is the conditioned one. The transmission must be in a format that maintains patient confidentiality and that can be read and stored in a retrievable and readable form.

Test the emailed image against that condition. A file the receiving system cannot store or later retrieve in readable form fails the storage and retrievability half of the test, whatever its appearance.

Note the additional conditions the same paragraph places on electronic transmission with electronic signatures: accord with M.G.L. c. 94C, § 23(g), 105 CMR 721.00, and 247 CMR 9.01(19) and 9.07(1)(a).
worked_examples.resolution: The indelible pencil referral satisfies the writing requirement and the emailed image does not. The error the scenario invites is treating the electronic document as the more compliant one because it looks more formal, when the electronic route is the route that carries conditions.

worked_examples.scenario: A collaborative practice agreement names three duties of the authorized pharmacist that may be delegated to appropriately trained staff and two duties that may not be delegated, and says nothing further on the subject. The pharmacist proposes to delegate one of the three named duties to a certified technician for the next six weeks, reasoning that the duty is on the permitted list and the technician is trained. What is still missing?
steps: Read 247 CMR 16.04(3) as two sentences rather than one. The first requires the agreement to specify the delegable duties and the duties that shall not be delegated; the agreement here satisfies that sentence.

Read the second sentence, which is the one the facts are aimed at: the agreement shall specify when and how an authorized pharmacist may delegate duties under the agreement, and the duration and scope of the delegation.

Match the proposal against it. A six-week delegation is a duration, but the duration has to be specified in the agreement rather than chosen afterwards by the pharmacist, and the when, the how and the scope are absent as well.

Resist the argument from competence. The staff member's training is a condition the regulation attaches to a delegation the agreement has authorised, not a substitute for the agreement authorising it.

Keep the ordinary scope rules in view: pharmacy intern and pharmacy technician duties supporting an authorized pharmacist under an agreement must still be performed in accordance with 247 CMR 8.01 and 8.02 through 8.06.
worked_examples.resolution: The agreement still lacks the when and how of delegation together with its duration and scope, so the delegation cannot go ahead on the present terms. The error the scenario invites is stopping at the first sentence of the paragraph and treating the naming of duties as the whole obligation.

worked_examples.scenario: During an inspection an authorized pharmacist produces the signed original agreement, which the supervising physician handed over for safekeeping, and nothing else. Asked for the patient referral and consent, the pharmacist says the physician keeps those. An investigator from the Board of Registration in Medicine then asks to see the file, and the pharmacist answers that the documents are retrievable only to the Board of Registration in Pharmacy. How many things have gone wrong?
steps: Identify what the pharmacist is required to hold under 247 CMR 16.04(6): a copy of the current collaborative practice agreement, including copies of the current patient referral and patient consent, in the primary practice setting.
Test the first answer. Holding the original is not compliance with a requirement to maintain a copy, and it also strips the physician's record of what the physician is required to keep.
Test the second. The referral and consent copies are part of the same obligation, so a file containing the agreement alone is incomplete even if the agreement itself is current.

Test the third. The copy must be readily retrievable at the request of the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and the Board of Registration in Medicine, so an answer limited to one board is wrong on its face.

Place the original where it belongs. In accordance with 243 CMR 2.12 the supervising physician must maintain the original of the current agreement, including the original current referral and consent, in the patient's medical record in the physician's own custody, so the transfer for safekeeping was not open to the parties to arrange.
worked_examples.resolution: Three things have gone wrong: the pharmacist holds the original instead of a copy, the referral and consent copies are missing, and retrievability was refused to one of the two boards entitled to ask. The error the scenario invites is treating custody as a housekeeping matter the two professionals may allocate between themselves.

worked_examples.scenario: A collaborative practice agreement lapses at the end of this month and will not be renewed. The pharmacist plans to write to each affected patient during the following week, explaining that the arrangement has ended and setting out how the patient's therapy will be continued, and considers that this discharges what is owed. Separately, the pharmacist resolved a Board matter last month by consent agreement that placed a condition on her practice, and she works under agreements with three supervising physicians. What has she missed?
steps: Split 247 CMR 16.04(5) into its two duties. Prior to termination or non-renewal, the pharmacist and the supervising physician shall arrange for an uninterrupted continuation of the patient's drug therapy in accordance with the terms of the agreement.

Read the second duty. When the agreement is not renewed or collaborative drug therapy management is otherwise terminated, the pharmacist and the supervising physician shall inform the patient in writing of the termination and of the procedures in place for continuation of the therapy.

Match the plan to the duties. The planned letter is the second duty and is timed correctly for it, but nothing in the plan is the arrangement for uninterrupted continuation, which was owed before the lapse.
Note that both duties are joint. They are owed by the authorized pharmacist and the supervising physician together, so a plan by the pharmacist alone does not discharge either of them.

Turn to the consent agreement. Under 247 CMR 16.02(3), discipline by the Board whether by agreement or Board order, and any other practice restriction, requires the pharmacist to provide written notification of the discipline or practice restriction to each supervising physician, which on these facts means three notifications rather than one.
worked_examples.resolution: She has missed the pre-termination arrangement for uninterrupted continuation of therapy, and she owes written notification of the consent agreement to each of her three supervising physicians. The error the scenario invites is twofold: seeing a written notice in the plan, matching it to the written-notice duty and stopping; and treating a matter resolved by agreement as something short of discipline.

worked_examples.scenario: A collaborating pharmacist completed her collaborative practice continuing education two years ago. Her current collaborative practice agreement was signed six months ago. She proposes to discard the course documentation on the ground that the courses themselves are now more than two years old, and adds that her pharmacist registration has been renewed since. May she?
steps: Locate the retention duty at 247 CMR 16.02(2): an authorized pharmacist participating in collaborative drug therapy management must maintain evidence of completion of required continuing education for at least two years after the date of the current collaborative practice agreement.
Fix the start of the clock. It runs from the date of the current agreement, not from the date of the course and not from any registration renewal.
Apply it. The current agreement is six months old, so the two-year period has eighteen months left to run and every piece of evidence for it is still inside the retention period.

Identify what is being retained: evidence of completion of the continuing education required for participation, which under 247 CMR 16.02(1)(e) is at least five additional contact hours of Board-approved continuing education in each year of the term of the agreement.
worked_examples.resolution: She may not discard the documentation; it must be kept for at least two years after the date of the current agreement. The error the scenario invites is measuring the retention period from the course date or from a registration renewal, either of which would release records the regulation still requires.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A collaborative practice agreement is a ______ and ______ agreement between which two parties?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Written and signed, between a pharmacist with training and experience relevant to the scope of the collaborative practice and a supervising physician, under M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(a) and restated at 247 CMR 16.04(1).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Whose scope of practice limits the collaborative practice an agreement may define?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The supervising physician's. The collaborative practice must be within the scope of the supervising physician's practice, so the agreement cannot reach past it.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How often must a collaborative practice agreement be reviewed and renewed, and by whom?
retrieval_prompts.answer: On a biennial basis under the statutory definition; 247 CMR 16.04(4) states it as at least every two years, by the authorized pharmacist and supervising physician or physicians themselves.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does the statutory definition require an agreement to include where the pharmacist is to prescribe?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Individually developed guidelines for any prescriptive practice of the pharmacist.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a referral written in indelible pencil fails the writing requirement.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. 243 CMR 2.12(1)(a) permits a paper-based document written in ink, indelible pencil or any other means, and names indelible pencil expressly.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the two qualities an electronically transmitted collaborative document's format must have.
retrieval_prompts.answer: It must maintain patient confidentiality, and it must be capable of being read and stored in a retrievable and readable form.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which external instruments must an electronic transmission with electronic signatures accord with?
retrieval_prompts.answer: M.G.L. c. 94C, § 23(g); 105 CMR 721.00; and 247 CMR 9.01(19) and 9.07(1)(a), with the information transmitted without alteration.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: List the four things 247 CMR 16.04(3) requires a collaborative practice agreement to specify about delegation.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The duties that may be delegated to other appropriately trained and authorized staff; the duties that shall not be delegated; when and how the authorized pharmacist may delegate; and the duration and scope of the delegation.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: An agreement is silent on delegation. May an appropriately trained technician take on one of the pharmacist's duties?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. Silence is not permission; the agreement must specify the delegable and non-delegable duties and the terms of delegation before any delegation power exists.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which party holds the original of the current agreement, and where must it be kept?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The supervising physician, in the patient's medical record in the physician's own custody, in accordance with 243 CMR 2.12.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What three documents must the authorized pharmacist maintain in the primary practice setting?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A copy of the current collaborative practice agreement, plus copies of the current patient referral and the current patient consent.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: At whose request must the pharmacist's copy be readily retrievable?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Both the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and the Board of Registration in Medicine.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which termination duty is owed before the agreement ends, and which is owed at the ending?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Before: arranging an uninterrupted continuation of the patient's drug therapy. At the ending: informing the patient in writing of the termination and of the continuation procedures. Both are owed jointly and in accordance with the terms of the agreement.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A Board matter is resolved by consent agreement with a condition on practice. What is owed, and to whom?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Written notification of the discipline or practice restriction to each supervising physician; discipline by agreement counts the same as a Board order.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Evidence of collaborative practice continuing education must be kept for how long, measured from what?
retrieval_prompts.answer: At least two years, measured from the date of the current collaborative practice agreement, not from the course date.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How many contact hours of continuing education does participation require, and over what period?
retrieval_prompts.answer: At least five additional contact hours of Board-approved continuing education in each year of the term of the agreement, addressing areas of practice generally related to the particular agreement, under 247 CMR 16.02(1)(e).

quick_review.text: A collaborative practice agreement is a written and signed agreement between a pharmacist with training and experience relevant to the scope of the collaborative practice and a supervising physician, defining the collaborative practice the two propose to engage in.
The collaborative practice defined by the agreement must be within the scope of the supervising physician's practice.

Each agreement is subject to review and renewal on a biennial basis; 247 CMR 16.04(4) puts the same duty as review and renewal by the authorized pharmacist and supervising physician or physicians at least every two years.
An agreement shall include individually developed guidelines for any prescriptive practice of the pharmacist.

For collaborative documents, written means, if paper based, written in ink, indelible pencil or any other means; or transmitted electronically in a format that maintains patient confidentiality and can be read and stored in a retrievable and readable form.

Electronic transmission with electronic signatures is permitted without alteration of the information, provided it accords with M.G.L. c. 94C, § 23(g), 105 CMR 721.00, and 247 CMR 9.01(19) and 9.07(1)(a).
The agreement must specify both the duties of the authorized pharmacist that may be delegated to other appropriately trained and authorized staff and those that shall not be delegated.
The agreement must also specify when and how an authorized pharmacist may delegate duties under it, and the duration and scope of the delegation; naming the duties alone is half the paragraph.
Pharmacy intern and pharmacy technician duties supporting an authorized pharmacist under an agreement must be performed in accordance with 247 CMR 8.01 and 8.02 through 8.06.

The authorized pharmacist maintains a copy of the current agreement, with copies of the current patient referral and patient consent, in the primary practice setting, readily retrievable at the request of the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and the Board of Registration in Medicine.
The supervising physician maintains the original of the current agreement, with the original current referral and consent, in the patient's medical record in the physician's custody.

Prior to termination or non-renewal, the authorized pharmacist and supervising physician shall arrange for an uninterrupted continuation of the patient's drug therapy, in accordance with the terms of the agreement.

When an agreement is not renewed or collaborative drug therapy management is otherwise terminated, the authorized pharmacist and supervising physician shall inform the patient in writing of the termination and of the procedures in place for continuation of the therapy.
Discipline by the Board, whether by agreement or Board order, and any other practice restriction, requires the authorized pharmacist to give written notification of it to each supervising physician.
Evidence of completion of required continuing education must be maintained for at least two years after the date of the current collaborative practice agreement.

Participation requires at least five additional contact hours of Board-approved continuing education in each year of the term of the agreement, addressing areas of practice generally related to the particular agreement.

decision_logic.condition: A set of facts asks whether a pharmacist may act under a collaborative practice agreement.
decision_logic.action: Test constitution first, then currency. Constitution: written, signed, the right two parties, and a collaborative practice inside the supervising physician's scope. Currency: reviewed and renewed within the last two years.

decision_logic.condition: The formation elements all check out and the facts give a date for the agreement.
decision_logic.action: Compute the interval since the last review and renewal. More than two years puts the agreement out of currency regardless of how well it was drafted, and a review that is only scheduled does not stop the clock.

decision_logic.condition: The agreement provides for the pharmacist to prescribe.
decision_logic.action: Check that individually developed guidelines for that prescriptive practice are included in the agreement itself; the further conditions attaching to prescriptive practice are treated in a separate section.

decision_logic.condition: A document is challenged as not being in writing.
decision_logic.action: Ask which route it took. If paper based, ink, indelible pencil or any other means will do. If electronic, test confidentiality, readability and storage in a retrievable and readable form, and then the accord with M.G.L. c. 94C, § 23(g), 105 CMR 721.00, and 247 CMR 9.01(19) and 9.07(1)(a).

decision_logic.condition: Somebody other than the authorized pharmacist is to perform a duty under the agreement.
decision_logic.action: Read the agreement for all four delegation elements before looking at the person. Absent any of them there is no delegation power, and the staff member's training does not create one.

decision_logic.condition: An inspector or investigator asks for the collaborative practice documents.
decision_logic.action: Produce the pharmacist's copy of the current agreement together with copies of the current referral and consent, from the primary practice setting, and produce them for the Board of Registration in Medicine as readily as for the Board of Registration in Pharmacy.

decision_logic.condition: A physician offers to leave the original agreement, referral or consent with the pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Decline the transfer. The original of each belongs in the patient's medical record in the custody of the supervising physician, and the pharmacist's obligation is discharged by a copy.

decision_logic.condition: An agreement is about to lapse, or either party proposes to end it.
decision_logic.action: Do the continuity work first, before the ending, jointly with the other party and on the terms the agreement itself sets; then, at the ending, send the patient a written notice covering both the termination and the continuation procedures.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacist in collaborative practice is disciplined or has any restriction placed on practice.
decision_logic.action: Count the supervising physicians and send each one a written notification of the discipline or practice restriction; a consent agreement is not an exemption, and neither is a restriction imposed outside a formal disciplinary process.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacist is deciding whether continuing education records may be destroyed.
decision_logic.action: Take the date of the current collaborative practice agreement, add two years, and keep everything until that date has passed; the course date and the registration renewal date are irrelevant to this calculation.

exceptions.text: The individually developed guidelines element of the statutory definition is conditioned on there being prescriptive practice: the agreement shall include individually developed guidelines for any prescriptive practice of the pharmacist, so an agreement with no prescriptive component is not defective for lacking them.

247 CMR 16.04(3) does not displace the ordinary scope rules for support staff. Pharmacy intern and pharmacy technician duties providing support to an authorized pharmacist acting under an agreement must still be performed in accordance with 247 CMR 8.01 for interns and 8.02 through 8.06 for technicians, so an agreement term cannot enlarge what those roles may do.

The writing definition is expressed as two alternatives rather than a single standard: a document satisfies it either by the paper route or by the electronic route, and failing the conditions attached to the electronic route does not convert the document into a compliant paper one.

timing_deadlines.event: Review and renewal of a collaborative practice agreement
timing_deadlines.timeframe: On a biennial basis; 247 CMR 16.04(4) states it as at least every two years
timing_deadlines.consequence: An agreement not reviewed and renewed within the period is no longer current, whatever its contents provide

timing_deadlines.event: Board-approved continuing education for collaborative practice
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At least five additional contact hours in each year of the term of the agreement
timing_deadlines.consequence: The continuing education required for participation is unmet, and there is nothing for the retention duty to preserve

timing_deadlines.event: Retention of evidence of completion of required continuing education
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At least two years after the date of the current collaborative practice agreement
timing_deadlines.consequence: Records discarded before that date are discarded early, even if the courses themselves are older than two years

timing_deadlines.event: Arranging an uninterrupted continuation of the patient's drug therapy
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Prior to termination or non-renewal of the agreement
timing_deadlines.consequence: A duty owed before the ending is missed, and no notice sent afterwards repairs it

timing_deadlines.event: Written notice to the patient of termination and of the continuation procedures
timing_deadlines.timeframe: When the agreement is not renewed, or collaborative drug therapy management is otherwise terminated
timing_deadlines.consequence: The patient is left without the written statement of the termination and of the arrangements now in place

timing_deadlines.event: Written notification of discipline or a practice restriction to each supervising physician
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Whenever the pharmacist is disciplined by the Board, whether by agreement or Board order, or is otherwise subject to any practice restriction
timing_deadlines.consequence: Each supervising physician not notified is a physician supervising in ignorance of a restriction on the pharmacist's practice

timing_deadlines.event: Production of the pharmacist's copy of the agreement, referral and consent
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Readily retrievable at the request of either board; the regulation sets a standard of retrievability rather than a period
timing_deadlines.consequence: A file that has to be assembled or fetched from elsewhere is not readily retrievable in the primary practice setting

timing_deadlines.event: Currency of the copies held by the pharmacist
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Continuously, for as long as the pharmacist acts under the agreement
timing_deadlines.consequence: A superseded agreement, referral or consent on file does not satisfy a requirement expressed in terms of the current documents

forms_records.text: The agreement itself: a written and signed instrument naming a pharmacist with training and experience relevant to the scope of the collaborative practice and a supervising physician, and defining the collaborative practice the two propose to engage in.
Where the agreement provides for the pharmacist to prescribe, it must carry individually developed guidelines for that prescriptive practice on its face.
A paper-based agreement, referral, consent or related document may be written in ink, indelible pencil or any other means.

An electronic agreement, referral, consent or related document must be in a format that maintains patient confidentiality and can be read and stored in a retrievable and readable form, may carry electronic signatures, must be transmitted without alteration of the information, and must accord with M.G.L. c. 94C, § 23(g), 105 CMR 721.00, and 247 CMR 9.01(19) and 9.07(1)(a).

The delegation terms are part of the agreement's own text: the delegable duties, the duties that shall not be delegated, when and how delegation may occur, and the duration and scope of the delegation.

The pharmacist's file in the primary practice setting: a copy of the current agreement, a copy of the current patient referral and a copy of the current patient consent, held so as to be readily retrievable at the request of the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and the Board of Registration in Medicine.

The physician's file: the original of the current agreement, together with the original current patient referral and patient consent, in the patient's medical record in the custody of the supervising physician.
The written notice to the patient on termination or non-renewal states two things, the termination itself and the procedures in place for the continuation of the patient's drug therapy.

The written notification of discipline or practice restriction is a separate document owed to each supervising physician, and its trigger is the discipline or restriction rather than anything happening to the agreement.
Evidence of completion of the required continuing education is retained by the pharmacist for at least two years after the date of the current collaborative practice agreement.

role_duties.role: Authorized pharmacist, as a party to the agreement
role_duties.duty: Enter only into a written and signed agreement whose defined collaborative practice sits inside the supervising physician's scope, and take part in reviewing and renewing it at least every two years.

role_duties.role: Supervising physician, as a party to the agreement
role_duties.duty: Confine the collaborative practice the agreement defines to the scope of the physician's own practice, and take part in the biennial review and renewal.

role_duties.role: Either party preparing a collaborative document
role_duties.duty: Produce it either on paper in ink, indelible pencil or any other means, or electronically in a confidential format that can be read and stored in a retrievable and readable form and that accords with the instruments 243 CMR 2.12(1)(b) names.
State the delegable duties, the duties that shall not be delegated, and when, how, for how long and how widely the authorized pharmacist may delegate.

Act only within delegation terms the agreement already contains, and only to appropriately trained and authorized staff, with intern and technician support kept inside 247 CMR 8.01 and 8.02 through 8.06.
Maintain a copy of the current agreement with copies of the current referral and consent in the primary practice setting, readily retrievable at the request of either board.
Maintain the original of the current agreement with the original current referral and consent in the patient's medical record in the physician's own custody.

role_duties.role: Board of Registration in Pharmacy and Board of Registration in Medicine
role_duties.duty: Either board may request the pharmacist's copy of the agreement, referral and consent, and the retrievability obligation runs to both of them equally.

role_duties.role: Authorized pharmacist and supervising physician, jointly, before an agreement ends
role_duties.duty: Arrange for an uninterrupted continuation of the patient's drug therapy, in accordance with the terms of the agreement.

role_duties.role: Authorized pharmacist and supervising physician, jointly, at the ending
role_duties.duty: Inform the patient in writing of the termination and of the procedures in place for the continuation of the patient's drug therapy.

role_duties.role: Authorized pharmacist who has been disciplined or restricted
role_duties.duty: Give written notification of the discipline or practice restriction to each supervising physician, counting consent agreements as discipline.

role_duties.role: Authorized pharmacist, as keeper of continuing education evidence
role_duties.duty: Complete at least five additional contact hours of Board-approved continuing education in each year of the term of the agreement and retain the evidence for at least two years after the date of the current agreement.

common_traps.text: Running the formation checklist, finding every element satisfied, and never asking when the agreement was last reviewed and renewed. Constitution and currency are separate tests and the second is the one that lapses quietly.
Adding a board filing step. Nothing in the definition makes the agreement effective on filing with a board; the filing the regulations require is filing a copy in the primary practice setting.

Reading the physician-scope limit as a formality. An agreement that defines a collaborative practice outside the supervising physician's own scope is defective in its definition, not merely ambitious.
Assuming the electronic document is the more compliant one because it looks more formal. The paper route carries almost no conditions and the electronic route carries all of them.
Rejecting indelible pencil as too informal, when the regulation names it in the same breath as ink.
Stopping after the first sentence of 247 CMR 16.04(3). Naming the delegable and non-delegable duties is half the paragraph; the when, the how, the duration and the scope are the other half.

Reasoning from the competence of the staff member rather than from the content of the agreement. Training is a condition on a delegation the agreement has authorised, not a source of authority in itself.
Holding the signed original on site and treating that as the more careful course. The pharmacist's obligation is to hold a copy, and the original belongs in the physician's record.
Producing the agreement without the referral and consent copies, or treating retrievability as owed to the Board of Registration in Pharmacy alone.
Collapsing the two termination duties into one notification after the ending. The continuity arrangement is owed before termination or non-renewal and is not discharged by any letter.
Assuming oral notice to the patient will do, or that the duties fall on the physician alone. The notice must be in writing and both duties are owed jointly.
Treating a matter resolved by consent agreement as something short of discipline, or notifying only the physician whose agreement relates to the conduct at issue.
Measuring the continuing education retention period from the course date or from the pharmacist's registration renewal instead of from the date of the current collaborative practice agreement.

sections.title: Prospective Drug Utilization Review and the Patient Profile It Runs On
sections.topic: Patient care / Prospective drug utilization review and the patient profile
sections.subtopic: The statutory prospective drug review in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A, the drug utilization review required by 247 CMR 9.17(1), the responsive-measure and documentation duties in 247 CMR 9.17(2), the current-standards requirement in 247 CMR 9.17(3), and the confidential patient profile, immediate-retrieval and reasonable-effort duties in 247 CMR 9.16(7) and 9.16(8)
learning_objectives: State the trigger for the prospective drug review in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A and the trigger for the drug utilization review in 247 CMR 9.17(1), and say precisely where the two differ.
Explain why the screening and identification lists attached to both mandates are permissive while the duty to conduct the review is not.
Set out what 247 CMR 9.16(7) requires a confidential patient profile to contain, and identify which of its duties is qualified by reasonable effort and which is not.
Apply the immediate-retrieval requirement to a pharmacy whose system cannot show previously dispensed drugs when the prescription is presented.
State the standard a drug utilization review must rest on under 247 CMR 9.17(3), and explain why a named work in a superseded edition can fail it while an unnamed current source can satisfy it.
Separate the discretionary choice of responsive measure in 247 CMR 9.17(2) from the mandatory record of whatever measure was taken.
Apply the inpatient carve-out in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A to a particular dispensing, and state what the carve-out attaches to.
Identify the exclusion in 247 CMR 9.16(8) and name the pharmacies it removes from 247 CMR 9.16.

orientation.text: Massachusetts imposes the prospective review twice, once by statute and once by regulation, and the two versions do not say quite the same thing. M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A opens by providing that a pharmacist shall conduct a prospective drug review before each new prescription is dispensed or delivered to a patient or a person acting on behalf of such patient. 247 CMR 9.17(1) provides that a pharmacist shall conduct a prospective drug utilization review, which the regulation abbreviates to DUR, before each new prescription or medication order is dispensed or delivered to a patient or a patient's agent. Both fix the moment of the duty at dispensing or delivery rather than at the moment the prescription arrives, and both reach a handover made to somebody other than the patient. The regulation is the wider of the two on its face, because it adds the medication order to the prescription. Neither provision makes the duty turn on how the prescription reached the pharmacy, and neither waits for the patient to ask.

What follows each mandate is a list, and in both places the list is the permissive half of the provision. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A the review may include, but not be limited to, screening for potential drug therapy problems due to therapeutic duplication, drug disease contraindication, drug interactions including serious interactions with nonprescription or over-the-counter drugs, incorrect drug dosage, duration of drug treatment, drug allergy interactions and clinical abuse or misuse. Under 247 CMR 9.17(1) the DUR may include a review of computerized alerts, the patient record, and each new and renewed prescription or medication order for the purpose of promoting therapeutic appropriateness, by making a reasonable effort to identify over-utilization or under-utilization, therapeutic duplication, drug-disease contraindication, drug-drug interaction, drug-food interaction, incorrect drug dosage or duration of drug treatment, drug-allergy interactions, abuse or misuse, any significant change in drug, dose, or directions, and any age related contraindications. The verb governing each list is may, while the verb governing the review itself is shall. Reading the list as the definition of the duty inverts the provision, and a pharmacist who has ticked every named item has not thereby answered the question the provision actually asks.

The review is not conducted on the prescription alone. 247 CMR 9.16(7) requires a pharmacist and pharmacy to maintain a confidential patient profile for each patient to whom a prescription is dispensed, and 247 CMR 9.17(1) names the patient record among the material a DUR may review. The profile is therefore the standing record the review runs on, and it is built before the individual dispensing rather than assembled at the counter. The pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee shall make a reasonable effort to obtain, record, and maintain the name, address, contact information, date of birth or age, and gender of the patient for whom the prescription is intended; the patient history, including known drug allergies and drug reactions; a comprehensive list of medications and relevant devices dispensed by the pharmacy; and the pharmacist's comments relevant to the patient's drug therapy.

Within that one paragraph sit two duties of different character, and the examinable point is that the qualifier on the first does not travel to the second. The content duty is qualified: the standard is a reasonable effort to obtain, record, and maintain, so an incomplete profile is not automatically a breach, and a pharmacy that simply never asked is not saved by the fact that the standard is effort rather than result. What is being graded is what the pharmacy did. The system duty carries no such qualifier. 247 CMR 9.16(7) provides flatly that the computerized pharmacy system shall provide for the immediate retrieval of information necessary for the pharmacist to identify previously dispensed drugs at the time the prescription is presented for dispensing. A system that surfaces that information only after an overnight batch, or only on a call to another office, does not meet it, and diligent questioning at the counter is not offered by the regulation as a substitute. 247 CMR 9.16(8) then removes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from the requirements in 247 CMR 9.16 altogether.

A review has to be measured against something, and 247 CMR 9.17(3) supplies the standard: the DUR shall be based upon current standards which may include the American Hospital Formulary Service Drug Information, the United States Pharmacopoeia Drug Information, the American Medical Association Drug Evaluations, Plumb's Veterinary Drug Handbook, and other peer-reviewed medical literature. Two features of that sentence do the work. The operative requirement is currency, carried by the word shall, so a source that is out of date fails whatever its title; and the list is open, both because it is introduced by may include and because its final item is a category rather than a work. A superseded edition of a named compendium is therefore not rescued by the fact that the compendium is named, and a current peer-reviewed source is not disqualified by the fact that it is not.

Finding something is not the end of the pharmacist's obligation. 247 CMR 9.17(2) provides that upon identifying any of the above, meaning any of the items the preceding paragraph lists, a pharmacist shall take appropriate measures to ensure the proper care of the patient, which may include consultation with the prescribing practitioner or direct consultation with the patient or patient's agent. The choice among measures belongs to the pharmacist, and the two named consultations are examples rather than a required sequence. The sentence that follows is not permissive at all: a pharmacist shall document any measures taken in response to a drug utilization review. That record duty stands on its own. It is owed on the measure taken rather than on the seriousness of the finding, and it is not discharged by resolving the clinical problem before anything is dispensed. Direct consultation with the patient under 247 CMR 9.17(2) is a response to a review finding, and it should not be confused with the separate offer-to-counsel regime, which other provisions carry and which this section does not treat.

One limit sits on the statutory duty and has to be placed accurately. The final paragraph of M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A provides that the provisions of that section shall not apply to any drug dispensed to an inpatient at a hospital or nursing home, except to the extent required by regulations promulgated by the Federal Health Care Financing Administration pursuant to 42 USC 1396r-8. Two things follow from the way it is worded. The carve-out attaches to the drug dispensed and to the patient's inpatient status, not to the pharmacy, its licence or its address, so a hospital pharmacy that also dispenses at an outpatient window is outside the carve-out for the outpatient dispensings it makes. And the carve-out names nursing homes alongside hospitals, so a candidate who remembers only the hospital half will misplace a nursing-home inpatient. The carve-out is stated in the statute, and it is not repeated in the text of 247 CMR 9.17.
